stage.name: Why is it called CVA6?
stage.description: A source-grounded microcourse for decoding CORE-V names without mistaking a name for a complete specification.

content.title: Why is it called CVA6?
content.subtitle: Read the family, class and pipeline clue, then verify the actual configuration.
content.thesis: CVA6 is a useful name, not a complete specification: CV identifies the family, A the application class, and 6 the pipeline depth named by the project.
content.narration: Why is the project called C V A six? The short answer is useful, but the engineering answer needs one extra caution. In the current CVA6 documentation, C V identifies the CORE-V family, A identifies the application class, and six points to a six-stage execution pipeline. The name gives us an orientation clue. It does not, by itself, tell us the exact instruction set, privilege modes, cache choices, issue width, or maturity of every configuration built from the repository.

content.narration: This lesson uses three evidence layers. First, the current CVA6 repository documentation is the authority for what C V, A and six mean in this project. Second, the current User Manual tells us what a named configuration actually implements and whether a name is still provisional. Third, an older public CORE-V deck explains the historical five-field syntax behind names such as C V thirty two E four zero P. That history is valuable, but current documentation wins whenever the two differ.

C V sixty four A six zero follows the current CVA6 part-number example: family, instruction length, class, pipeline stages, and product identifier. content.narration: There are two related naming layers. The current CVA6 page gives a compact rule for cores derived from this repository: C V, instruction length, class, pipeline stages, and a product identifier. The older CORE-V deck used a broader five-field structure that also named identity and modifier fields. These models overlap, but they should not be forced into one universal grammar. This is why the lesson labels the older decomposition as historical context and keeps the current project documentation as the authority.

anchor.label: Engineering sentence
anchor.text: Never transfer a feature from one CVA6 configuration to another without checking the configuration table.

content.narration: The most important distinction is project versus product instance. CVA6 is the repository and configurable code base. The documentation says the repository as-is is not one specific production core. A name such as C V thirty two A six zero X points to configuration-specific evidence. That evidence can define instruction extensions, privilege modes, interfaces, issue direction, and maturity. A feature found in one configuration should never be copied automatically to every CVA6 variant.

content.narration: Three examples show why names are clues rather than contracts. C V sixty four A six zero is the example on the current nomenclature page. C V thirty two A six zero X is a real configuration name, but the current introduction calls that part number interim while the team decides the issue direction. C V thirty two E four zero P is historically easy to decompose, yet its implemented behavior and released parameter sets must come from the current CV32E40P manual. A readable name is not a frozen product definition.

scenes.title: What the name does not prove

content.sceneTitle: What the name does not prove
content.title: What the name does not prove
content.subtitle: Do not infer architecture details that the current configuration documents have not confirmed.

items.title: ISA extensions
items.body: The name does not enumerate I, M, A, C, bit-manipulation, vector, or custom extensions.

items.title: Privilege modes
items.body: Machine-only and Linux-capable configurations can live in the same repository family.

items.title: Issue width
items.body: A six-stage name does not, by itself, prove single- or dual-issue behavior.

items.title: Memory system
items.body: MMU, PMP, caches, interfaces, and sizes remain configuration questions.

items.title: Maturity
items.body: A part number does not automatically prove RTL freeze, TRL level, release, or verification coverage.

items.title: Future stability
items.body: Product identifiers can be interim and naming practice can evolve.

content.takeaway: A good reader extracts the clue, then opens the configuration evidence before making a technical claim.
content.narration: Here is the boundary to remember. The name does not list the implemented ISA extensions. It does not prove privilege modes, cache organization, M M U or P M P support, issue width, verification coverage, or maturity. Even the six in CVA6 is a pipeline clue, not a performance score. The name is excellent for navigation: it narrows the family, width, class, or pipeline direction. Engineering conclusions begin only after the configuration table, design documentation, and release evidence agree.

content.title: Decode, then verify
content.subtitle: This sequence works for students, integrators, and verification engineers.

steps.title: Parse
steps.body: Extract only the fields the current source explicitly defines.

steps.title: Identify
steps.body: Decide whether the name refers to a repository, family, product, or configuration.

steps.title: Confirm
steps.body: Check ISA, privilege, interfaces, issue width, and memory-system details.

steps.title: Qualify
steps.body: Check release, maturity, verification scope, and whether the identifier is provisional.

content.takeaway: Names accelerate navigation. Documentation supplies the contract.
content.narration: Use a four-step habit. First, parse only the fields that an official source defines. Second, identify the object: repository, family, product, or configuration. Third, confirm instruction set, privilege modes, interfaces, issue width, and memory system in the configuration documents. Fourth, qualify the claim with release and maturity evidence. This conservative habit lets a beginner read names confidently without giving an expert a misleading shortcut.

content.narration: The durable takeaway is simple. C V identifies the CORE-V family. In CVA6, A means application class and six names the six-stage pipeline. CVA6 itself is a configurable repository and project, not one immutable production core. Historical naming diagrams can explain how labels such as C V thirty two E four zero P were formed, but current manuals decide present behavior. Read the name for orientation, then read the configuration and release evidence before making a technical claim.
